title: Tarn Taran
hookLine: Guru Arjan's town with one of the largest pools

lines: THE GURU IS THE POOL OF NECTAR.
THE TOWN IS A POOL FIRST.
cards: The Guru is the place of pilgrimage. The Guru is the pool of nectar. That's a paraphrase of a line by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Hold it while you stand at the edge of the water at Tarn Taran. The pool is so wide the far side looks small, and the walkway around it, the parikrama, feels like a long evening walk.
Along one side, the gurdwara's reflection lies on the water. Guru Arjan made this place. Today: why the town is a pool first.

teach.b: Start with the builder. Tradition says Guru Arjan founded Tarn Taran and had its sarovar dug, a pool for bathing and gathering, with the gurdwara beside it. Then the name.

Tradition explains Tarn Taran as the boat that carries across, a raft over the world's rough water, so the name points past the water to the crossing. Then the line from the hook, in fuller paraphrase.

teach.h: THE GURU IS THE POOL OF NECTAR.
teach.b: Guru Arjan writes that the Guru is mother and father, the place of pilgrimage and the pool of nectar, and that bathing in the Guru's wisdom is beyond measure.
So the pool at Tarn Taran is a real pool, with real water and real bathers, and also a picture of the Guru's wisdom, wide enough for anyone to step into. Then the people.
Tradition says Guru Arjan cared here for people with leprosy, people other towns turned away.
A wide pool, and a wide welcome. This is the week's last place, so look back down the road: Panja Sahib, the handprint. Anandpur, the city of bliss.
Fatehgarh, the young martyrs. Muktsar, the paper torn up. Goindval, the steps down to the water.
Khadur, the letters and the kitchen.
And Tarn Taran, the wide pool. Place after place, something ordinary, water, a hand, a paper, a kitchen, a board of letters, turned toward God.

how: Pilgrims at Tarn Taran Sahib walk the parikrama around the wide sarovar, bathe in it, and bow at the gurdwara Guru Arjan founded.

games.why: both: real water, real bathers, and a picture of the Guru's wisdom, wide enough for anyone.

practice: Picture water stretching out so wide the far side looks small, with a walkway of white stone all the way around, and begin to walk it slowly in your mind, the water on your right.
Let the people you pass be all kinds, old, young, sick, well, strangers, with room at the edge for all of them, and keep walking and breathing.
